summary: A 1970 report on a network meeting, written by Jon Postel. It records the discussion.

plainLanguage.summary: A write-up of what was discussed at a meeting.

subtitle: A report on the November 1970 network research meetings at the FJCC in Houston.

tldr.problem: The early ARPA network community needed to coordinate on protocol improvements, identify critical missing features, and align on development priorities.
tldr.mechanism: Three meetings were held at the Fall Joint Computer Conference where the Network Working Group discussed seven major topics including protocol testing, TELNET, documentation, graphics, and accounting, with detailed debate on console interaction models.
tldr.outcome: The meetings established a pattern of coordinated design decisions, prioritized TELNET development, set expectations for the Network Information Center, and influenced the direction of network standards development.

today: RFC 77 is an Internet Experiment document. It is historically significant as a detailed record of early network governance and decision-making, showing how the community coordinated development during the critical formative period of the ARPA network.

sections.title: The Meeting Overview
sections.content:
RFC 77, written by Jon Postel, reports on three days of meetings held November 16-18, 1970, at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in Houston. The meetings were chaired by Steve Crocker and brought together the Network Working Group to discuss practical issues and coordinate development.

The group identified seven major topics of concern: protocol testing, host-host protocol improvements, TELNET specification, documentation, graphics, measurement and statistics, and resource accounting.
sections.plainLanguage: The network builders met for three days and made a list of the most important things they needed to work on.

sections.title: Key Decisions and Discussions
sections.content:
The group decided that protocol changes should happen in bunches at roughly six-month intervals rather than continuously, with a three-month lead time for implementation. They approved a proposed IMP-Host protocol change to eliminate marking, though implementation would be delayed. The meetings emphasized that the network must be used to gain operational experience and that console-level TELNET should take priority over graphics development.

A significant focus was the Network Information Center (NIC), presented by Doug Engelbart of SRI. The group discussed plans for NIC to make network and host system documentation available online, representing an early vision of networked information sharing. The meetings also covered the differences between half/full duplex and character/line-oriented console systems, recognizing the challenge of supporting diverse host systems.
sections.plainLanguage: They agreed to make changes carefully in batches, focus on getting remote login working before graphics, and build a system to share documentation about all the computers on the network.

sections.title: Direction and Impact
sections.content:
The meetings established patterns that shaped network development: coordination through regular meetings, prioritization of practical features over experimental ones, and emphasis on documentation and shared knowledge. The decisions influenced immediate priorities (TELNET development, NIC formation) and set expectations for the pace and scope of protocol evolution.

The report demonstrates the collaborative nature of early ARPA network development and how design decisions emerged from discussion among implementers at different sites rather than top-down specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The meetings showed how the network builders worked together to decide what to build next, and these decisions shaped how the network grew.
